claims.note: The article is unread. FB4's parameter file does hold four striped bass rows credited to 'Hartman and Brandt 1995' (adult, age-0, age-1, age-2; see notes), so the attribution follows FB4. NOTE FOR THE REWRITE: the model does not use this surrogate — src/species.js:333-341 runs white perch on FB4's yellow perch sets (Kitchell et al. 1977) after the striped bass rows starved white perch over winter. Table 3.5-3 should say which set the model uses, or say 'striped bass suggested; yellow perch used'.

claims.claim: the striped bass rows (Hartman & Brandt 1995): their Thornton–Lessem curve all but stops consumption below ~6 °C; Cmax for a 100-g fish at 18.5 °C 0.093 g/g/d (the striper set) against the perch set's 0.061
claims.note: Unchecked against the article. Redone from FB4's stored rows (my arithmetic, CEQ 3 Thornton–Lessem): the temperature multiplier F(T) is 0.017/0.057/0.169 at 2/4/6 °C (adult row), 0.054/0.112/0.219 (age-1), 0.044/0.099/0.209 (age-2), 0.038/0.076/0.145 (age-0) — so 'all but stops' fits ≤ 4 °C better than 6 °C (15–22 % of the maximum remains at 6 °C). Cmax at 18.5 °C for 100 g: 0.094 (adult), 0.092 (age-1), 0.093 (age-2), 0.089 (age-0); FB4's yellow perch adult row 0.061. The code's 0.093 is the age-2 row. The abstract (Crossref) adds a caveat that bears on the winter failure: in laboratory validation 'at 6.9 °C consumption by striped bass was overestimated by 20–46%'.

FB4 credits its 'Weakfish (juvenile & adult)' row (CA 0.492, CB −0.268, CQ 14.8, CTO 25, CTM 25, CTL 29, CK1 0.195, CK4 0.97; RA 0.003, RB −0.155, RQ 0.0508, RTO 0.9022; ED 5860) to 'Hartman and Brandt 1996', not 1995 — check which paper prints it. Reading the REQ-1 rows (FB4 User's Guide p. 13): with RTL 0, RK1 1, RK4 0, RK5 0, swimming speed is a constant 1 cm/s, so RTO acts as a fixed activity multiplier, e^RTO (striped bass adult 1.65, age-0 2.46; bluefish 1.88; weakfish age-0 3.43). Every row shares one Cmax weight function (CA 0.3021, CB −0.2523 for all striped bass ages) and varies only the temperature curve with age, which matches the abstract's finding that 'Temperature effects on maximum consumption rate (Cmax) differed with fish size'. The abstract also says Cmax of young (30-g) fish rose with temperature then 'declined rapidly at higher temperatures', while larger fish (100–3000 g) levelled off at 25–30 °C.
